hook: Two thousand years ago a man wrote his friend a letter that just said: I'm not ill, and I'm not well.
story: His name was Serenus. He wasn't in crisis. Nothing had collapsed. He just couldn't tell if anything was wrong. So he wrote to Seneca and tried to describe it: I am neither sick nor well. Then this: I am distressed, not by a tempest, but by sea-sickness. No storm. Just the sway.
lesson: If you've been flat for weeks and can't point at a reason, that's it. It has a name and it's old. Seneca didn't tell him to toughen up. He wrote him a whole book back. Tonight, do the Serenus thing. Text one person the actual sentence: I'm not bad, I'm just off.
quote: I am neither sick nor well.
author: Serenus, quoted by Seneca
citation: De Tranquillitate Animi I, trans. Aubrey Stewart
tonight: Text one person: "I'm not bad, I'm just off."
broll: a man lying awake in a dark bedroom
a phone screen glowing at night
calm open sea from a boat deck
a hand holding a phone, unsent message

hook: Marcus Aurelius broke down crying in public when his teacher died, and the palace staff moved in to stop him.
story: Marcus was young. His tutor died and he wept where people could see it, and the court officials closed in to shut it down. Then the emperor, his adoptive father, stopped them with one sentence: Let him be only a man for once; for neither philosophy nor empire takes away natural feeling.
lesson: That is the head of the Roman Empire telling a room full of men to leave a crying boy alone. Two thousand years of people using Stoicism to mean don't feel it, and it starts with an emperor saying the opposite. You're allowed. Tonight, if something's sitting in your throat, stop swallowing it. Nobody's grading you.
quote: Let him be only a man for once; for neither philosophy nor empire takes away natural feeling.
author: Antoninus Pius
citation: Recorded in the Historia Augusta, Life of Antoninus Pius 10.5, trans. David Magie
caveat: The Historia Augusta is a late and sometimes unreliable source. Say 'recorded in the Historia Augusta', never 'Marcus wrote'.
tonight: Stop swallowing the thing in your throat.
broll: marble hall in low light
a young man alone turning away
rain on a stone step at dusk
candle burning low in a dark room

hook: Epictetus had one rule for the person you've stopped speaking to. It's about which end you pick it up by.
story: He said everything you're carrying has two handles. One you can lift. One you can't. If your brother's done you wrong and you pick the thing up by he wronged me, that handle breaks in your hand every time. You've probably proved that already.
lesson: So he says grab the other one: that he is your brother, that he was brought up with you. That's not forgiveness. That's choosing which end to hold so you can actually move it. If there's a message you've left sitting for weeks, the shame is why it's heavy, not the message. Send four words tonight. Been meaning to reply.
quote: Everything has two handles, the one by which it may be borne, the other by which it may not.
author: Epictetus
tonight: Send four words: "Been meaning to reply."
broll: two hands lifting a heavy clay jar
an unanswered message on a phone
two brothers walking apart on a street
a doorway left open at night

hook: A Roman official admitted that when his daughter got sick, he ran out of the house. He couldn't watch.
story: He left. He stayed away until someone came and told him she was better. She recovered. And he was so ashamed of himself that he brought it to a philosopher. Epictetus didn't call him a coward. He asked one question: would you call it love if her mother had done it?
lesson: He hadn't loved her less. He'd run from the feeling instead of standing in it. That's the whole gap. Most of us aren't cold, we're overwhelmed, and then we're ashamed of leaving. If you walked out on something hard today, you're not a bad man. Go back in tomorrow. That's the entire repair.
quote: Convince me that you acted naturally, and I will convince you that everything which takes place according to nature takes place rightly.
author: Epictetus
caveat: Epictetus does argue the man was wrong. Do NOT include that beat - the script sails on 'he loved her, he was overwhelmed'.
tonight: Go back into the room you walked out of.
broll: empty hospital corridor at night
a father sitting in a parked car
a child's bedroom door ajar
dawn light through a kitchen window

hook: Marcus Aurelius ran the Roman Empire, and kept writing himself notes about not wanting to get out of bed.
story: In his private notebook, this: In the morning when thou risest unwillingly, let this thought be present. I am rising to the work of a human being. Read it again. He's arguing with himself. He even writes the other side's lines: but this is more pleasant. That's a man losing to his own blankets, in ink, as emperor.
lesson: Meditations isn't a book of answers. It's twenty years of the same man failing at the same small thing and writing the note again. He never fixed it. He just kept writing it. Tonight, write one line for tomorrow morning. One. Then sleep.
quote: In the morning when thou risest unwillingly, let this thought be present: I am rising to the work of a human being.
author: Marcus Aurelius
tonight: Write one line for tomorrow morning. Then sleep.
broll: unmade bed in grey morning light
a hand writing in a worn notebook
oil lamp on a desk before dawn
a man sitting on the edge of a bed

hook: Marcus Aurelius wrote down that he had failed at becoming a philosopher, while he was Emperor of Rome.
story: The opening of book eight. He tells himself it's obvious to everyone how far he is from the life he meant to live, and that he'll probably never be called a philosopher. Then, instead of a plan, he gives himself permission: stop caring how it looks, and live the rest of it the way your nature wants.
lesson: That's the Emperor of Rome writing off the version of himself he'd promised. He was nearly fifty. He did the job anyway for another ten years. If you're carrying a version of yourself you didn't become, you're allowed to put him down. Tonight, name him once, out loud. I'm not him.
quote: Be content then in the rest of thy life, and let nothing else distract thee.
author: Marcus Aurelius
tonight: Say the name of the man you didn't become. Then say "I'm not him."
broll: a man looking at his reflection in a dark window
an old photograph face down
empty office at night
long road at dusk

hook: Seneca wrote the rulebook on how to grieve properly. Then his closest friend died and he did all of it wrong, and published that.
story: He'd written the advice. Don't be undone. Keep your feet. Then Annaeus Serenus died, younger than him, and Seneca fell apart. He put it in a letter, in public, under his own name. He said he wept so much that he must be counted among the examples of men who have been overcome by grief.
lesson: The most quoted man in Rome, filing himself in the failure column. He kept writing for years after. He was alright. If you didn't handle something the way you meant to, that doesn't cancel you. Tonight, say the name of whoever you lost. Just the name. That's allowed to be the whole thing.
quote: I wept so excessively for my dear friend that I must be included among the examples of men who have been overcome by grief.
author: Seneca
citation: Moral Letters 63.14, trans. Richard M. Gummere
caveat: Never schedule within two weeks of serenus_not_ill - same Serenus, and this reveals his death.
tonight: Say the name out loud. Just the name.
broll: empty chair by a window
rain on a dark street
a man alone at a table
candle going out

hook: A famous Stoic went white with fear in a storm at sea, and a rich passenger mocked him for it afterwards.
story: A Roman on that ship wrote it down. The philosopher didn't scream. But he went pale, and everyone saw. When the sea calmed, a wealthy Greek came over to needle him about it. The philosopher just pulled a book out of his bag, Epictetus, and showed him the passage.
lesson: The first hit lands on everyone. The body goes before the mind gets a vote. What makes you steady isn't never flinching. It's not agreeing with the flinch. So when your chest goes tight tonight for no reason, that's the first hit. It isn't cowardice. Put a hand flat on your chest and let it pass. It does.
quote: He is affected for a short time and slightly in his colour and expression, but does not assent.
author: Aulus Gellius
citation: Attic Nights 19.1, trans. John C. Rolfe
tonight: Hand flat on your chest. Let the first hit pass.
broll: storm waves against a ship hull
a man gripping a railing at sea
dark clouds over open water
calm sea after a storm

hook: Seneca put himself on trial every night before sleep, and wrote down the verdict he always handed himself.
story: He got it from his teacher Sextius, who asked himself at lights-out: what bad habit did you cure today? Seneca did the same. He replayed the day. Then this: I conceal nothing from myself, and omit nothing. Why should I be afraid of any of my shortcomings, when it is in my power to say, I pardon you this time, see that you never do that anymore?
lesson: He pardons himself. Every night. That's the part everyone leaves out. If you snapped at someone today and you've been chewing it since four o'clock, do the whole practice, not half. Look at it. Then say: pardoned. Not again. Sleep.
quote: I pardon you this time: see that you never do that anymore.
author: Seneca
citation: On Anger III.36, trans. Aubrey Stewart
tonight: Replay it once. Then say: "Pardoned. Not again."
broll: a man switching off a bedside lamp
hands washing a face in a dim bathroom
notebook closing
dark bedroom ceiling

hook: Seneca was one of the richest men in Rome, and still went red in the face when a better-off group rode past him.
story: He was travelling rough on purpose, a farm cart, a mattress on the ground. Then a wealthier party rode by, and he felt his face go hot. He was in his sixties. He was the most famous philosopher alive. And he wrote it down: whenever we meet a more sumptuous party I blush in spite of myself.
lesson: Then he named what it was. Not a sin, just proof that the thing he believed hadn't fully moved in yet. That's all it is when you feel behind your friends. Not weakness. Unfinished. Tonight, when you catch yourself measuring, say the word unfinished, out loud if you can. Then let it go.
quote: Whenever we meet a more sumptuous party I blush in spite of myself.
author: Seneca
citation: Moral Letters 87.4, trans. Richard M. Gummere
tonight: When you catch yourself comparing, say one word: "unfinished."
broll: a slow cart on a country road
expensive cars passing at night
a man watching from a roadside
dust settling on a track

hook: Someone told Seneca he had no right to give anyone advice, given the state of his own life. Seneca agreed with him.
story: Lucilius called him out: you're telling me how to live and you haven't sorted yourself. Seneca didn't argue. He wrote: I am not so shameless as to undertake to cure my fellow-men when I am ill myself. And then, he's sharing the remedy just as if we were lying ill in the same hospital.
lesson: Same hospital. Not doctor and patient. Two men in the ward. If you've been quietly disqualifying yourself from helping your mate, from starting again, from calling anyone, because you're not fixed yet, that rule is invented. Nobody's fixed. Tonight, say the thing you'd say to a friend, to yourself, in his voice.
quote: I am sharing the remedy with you, just as if we were lying ill in the same hospital.
author: Seneca
citation: Moral Letters 27.1, trans. Richard M. Gummere
tonight: Say to yourself, in the voice you'd use on a friend, the thing you'd tell him.
broll: two beds in a dim room
a man writing a letter by lamplight
hospital window at night
two chairs facing each other

hook: A philosopher walked into an advancing army to talk them out of the war. They laughed at him until he gave up and walked away.
story: Rome, sixty-nine AD. Musonius Rufus joined a peace delegation, walked in among armed soldiers, and argued the blessings of peace and the perils of war. Tacitus records it: many thought it ridiculous, more thought it tiresome, and some were ready to knock him down, so he stopped. He walked away having achieved nothing, in front of everyone.
lesson: Then he went home and kept teaching, and one of the young men in his room became Epictetus. Everything you know from Epictetus came through a man who'd been laughed out of a field. The worst thing you did in front of people is not the last thing about you.
quote: Many thought it ridiculous, more thought it tiresome.
author: Tacitus
citation: Histories III.81, trans. Church and Brodribb
tonight: Name the humiliation once, in the past tense.
broll: a lone figure facing a crowd
dust on a roman road
a man walking away across a field
a teacher with students in a small room

hook: Zeno lost an entire ship's cargo at thirty and washed up broke in a strange city. What he did that afternoon started Stoicism.
story: He was a merchant, not a philosopher. Purple dye, a full ship, gone. He came up into Athens, wandered into a bookseller's shop and started reading. It was Xenophon, about Socrates. He looked up and asked the bookseller where he could find men like that. The bookseller pointed at a man walking past and said, follow him. He did.
lesson: Later he said: I made a prosperous voyage when I suffered shipwreck. Not a lesson, just what happened. Losing the thing isn't always the end of the story. Sometimes it's the part before it. Tonight, one thing you lost this year. Ask what it made room for. Don't force an answer.
quote: I made a prosperous voyage when I suffered shipwreck.
author: Zeno of Citium
citation: Diogenes Laertius, Lives VII.4, trans. R. D. Hicks
caveat: Diogenes Laertius gives two versions. Say 'the story goes', not 'we know'.
tonight: Name one thing you lost this year. Ask what it made room for.
broll: wrecked cargo on a shore
an old bookshop interior
a man reading alone
harbour at first light

hook: Seneca spent a whole letter proving a strong mind can work through unbearable noise. The last line is him admitting he moved out.
story: He was living above a public bath. He lists all of it: men grunting under weights, the slap of a massage, the drinks seller shouting, and the man whose armpits are being plucked, screaming. Then he argues, brilliantly, that a settled mind doesn't need quiet. And at the end he just says: why should I torment myself any longer, when the fix is this easy?
lesson: He wanted to test himself. He'd tested himself. He left. You don't get points for enduring something you're allowed to change. Tonight, pick the one thing you've been white-knuckling that has an actual door. Don't solve it. Just admit out loud that the door exists.
quote: Why need I be tormented any longer?
author: Seneca
citation: Moral Letters 56.15, trans. Richard M. Gummere
tonight: Name the thing you've been enduring that has a door.
broll: noisy street seen from a window
a man packing a single bag
an open door in a dark hallway
quiet room at last

hook: Someone stole Epictetus's lamp in the night. His reaction has irritated people for two thousand years.
story: He kept an iron lamp beside his household gods. One night he heard a noise at the window, ran down, and it was gone. He didn't rage. He said the reason he lost the lamp was that the thief was better than him at staying awake, and that the thief paid for it by becoming a thief. Tomorrow, he said, buy an earthenware one.
lesson: That's it. No lesson about the universe. He was better at staying up, I'll get a cheaper lamp. Most of what's eating you tonight is lamp-sized. Pick one thing you're still angry about that cost under fifty bucks. Say earthenware, and drop it.
quote: The reason why I lost my lamp was that the thief was superior to me in vigilance.
author: Epictetus
tonight: Pick one grudge that cost under fifty bucks. Say "earthenware."
broll: an old oil lamp burning
an empty shelf at night
a shuttered window
a plain clay lamp on a table
